Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

This calendar booking API lets you create, read, update, and cancel bookings across one or more calendars. It handles time zone conversion, recurring events, and availability checks, so your application can offer scheduling without building that logic from scratch.

Every booking belongs to a calendar and includes a start time, end time, and a list of attendees. The API checks for conflicts when you create or move a booking and returns a 409 status with the conflicting event if the requested slot is unavailable. You can override this check with the `force` parameter, though we recommend against it for user-facing booking flows.

Authentication uses OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens scoped to a single calendar or a full account, depending on how you register your application. Rate limits are 100 requests per minute per token, returned in the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header on every response.

The guide covers the five core endpoints — list, create, get, update, and delete — along with webhook subscriptions for booking changes and a reference for the error codes you'll encounter. Each section includes request and response examples in curl and in the two official client libraries, for JavaScript and Python.

If you're integrating a scheduling widget or building booking logic into an existing product, start with the Quickstart section. It walks through creating your first booking end to end, from authentication to confirmation.

This API lets your application manage calendar bookings without you having to write that logic yourself. Instead of talking directly to a database or a calendar app, your code sends requests over the internet to our servers, and our servers send back the answer. Each request is a small, structured message: create a booking, look one up, change it, or cancel it.

A booking has three required pieces: the calendar it belongs to, a start and end time, and a list of attendees. Send those to the API and it creates the booking. If the time slot is already taken, the API tells you so, rather than silently double-booking someone.

Before you can use the API, you need a token, a long string of characters that proves your application is allowed to make requests. You get one by registering your application, and every request you send must include that token. Tokens also come with a limit: 100 requests per minute. Each response tells you how many requests you have left, so you can pace your application accordingly.

The rest of the guide walks through the requests you'll send most often: listing bookings, creating one, fetching details, updating a time, and canceling. Start with the Quickstart section. It walks you through creating your first booking step by step, using nothing more than a web browser and a tool called curl to send requests.
